unit_label: Module D unit 7 (courseware unit 32): fraud and vigilance in banks

facts.statement: Fraud and its legal definitions (courseware): fraud is an intentional deception to secure unfair or unlawful gain, directly or indirectly, and can be civil wrongdoing or a criminal offence depending on context and severity. Under section 17 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, fraud includes acts committed by a party to a contract, or with connivance or by an agent, with intent to deceive another party or induce entry into the contract: (i) the suggestion, as a fact, of that which is not true by one who does not believe it to be true; (ii) the active concealment of a fact by one having knowledge or belief of it; (iii) a promise made without any intention of performing it; (iv) any other act fitted to deceive; and (v) any act or omission the law specially declares fraudulent. Mere silence is not fraud unless the circumstances make it the person's duty to speak or the silence is in itself equivalent to speech. Under the explanation to section 447 of the Companies Act, 2013, fraud in relation to the affairs of a company includes any act, omission, concealment of any fact or abuse of position committed by any person or any other person with the connivance in any manner, with intent to deceive, to gain undue advantage from, or to injure the interests of, the company or its shareholders or creditors or any other person, whether or not there is any wrongful gain or loss; wrongful gain is gain by unlawful means of property to which the person gaining is not legally entitled and wrongful loss is loss by unlawful means of property to which the person losing is legally entitled. The Indian Penal Code, 1860 (section 25) defined "fraudulently" as doing a thing with intent to defraud but not otherwise; this definition is now section 2(9) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which replaced the IPC from 1 July 2024. Intent to defraud is of paramount importance; defraud means deceit and injury.

facts.statement: Forgery (courseware, IPC-era account): forgery generally means forging a document, that is creating a false written document or altering a genuine one with intent to defraud. The courseware says the offence of making a false document is complete as soon as the document is made with intent to commit fraud; the document need not be in the name of an existing person (a fictitious or deceased person suffices); if several persons combine to forge an instrument and each takes a distinct part, all are guilty; counterfeiting a document to support a legal claim is forgery; antedating becomes forgery if the date is material; a document made to conceal a previous fraudulent or dishonest act is forgery, but falsification only to conceal a previous negligent act is not; a man's signature of his own name may amount to forgery; the offence of forgery can be abetted; and affixing an electronic signature has the meaning in clause (d) of sub-section (1) of section 2 of the Information Technology Act, 2000. The IPC sections the courseware cites (463 forgery; 464 making a false document) correspond to sections 336(1) and 335 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 from 1 July 2024.
facts.locator: S01 printed pp. 671-672; BNS 336(1) and 335 from the NCRB correspondence table

facts.statement: Areas in which frauds are committed (courseware): deposits: fraudulent documentation (altering or modifying a document, or giving information knowingly wrong); deposit accounts with lax KYC or inoperative accounts are vulnerable; staff who keep original fixed deposit receipts and hand over fake photocopies, then misuse the original FDs by forging signatures for granting fictitious loans or transferring funds before maturity. Advances: frauds by unscrupulous borrowers (companies, partnership or proprietorship firms and their directors or partners) by methods such as fraudulent discounting of instruments (kite flying in clearing), fraudulent removal or disposal of hypothecated stocks and inflating stock statements, diversion of funds outside the borrowing unit, falsification of documents (false financial information), forged export documents (airway bills, bills of lading, ECGC guarantee cover, customs numbers) and identity theft; banks exercise due diligence on borrowers, promoters and associates, and third parties such as builders, warehouse and cold storage owners, vehicle and tractor dealers, travel agents and professionals (architects, valuers, chartered accountants, advocates) are held accountable if they played a vital role in sanction, disbursement or the fraud. Transactional areas: counterfeit or fake cheques (overpayment, internet auction and secret shopper scams); mobile banking applications mapped to a wrong mobile number; fake non-existent users created on third-party mobile platforms; SIM cloning and SIM swap; unauthorised deductions from mobile wallets (including dormant accounts); failure of due diligence on merchants; debit card skimming; ATM fraud; triangulation or site cloning; UPI request-money frauds; impersonation or identity theft; and fraud through installation of remote access software (for example Anydesk and TeamViewer). The courseware also gives fraud statistics from the RBI Annual Report 2024-25 (not taught).

Cyber threats (courseware): a cyber-attack is an intentional, malicious effort by an organisation or an individual to breach another's systems, with motives such as information theft, financial gain, espionage or sabotage. The main types: distributed denial of service (DDoS: overwhelming the target's resources so that it stops functioning, often as a diversion for more subtle attacks); social engineering (psychologically manipulating users, including phishing, spear phishing and homograph attacks); man-in-the-middle (attackers insert themselves between user and server, including session hijacking, replay, IP spoofing and eavesdropping attacks); malware and spyware (Trojan virus, ransomware that blocks access to data and threatens deletion or publication unless a ransom is paid, and malvertising: malicious code in online advertising); password attacks (sniffing, social engineering, guessing or accessing a password database); and advanced persistent threats (APT: unauthorised network access that remains undiscovered for a long time to exfiltrate sensitive data, typically against nation states or large corporations). Ransomware and identity theft are the two other major cyber threats the courseware stresses; crypto ransomware encrypts valuable files; computers are commonly infected through phishing e-mail attachments or links, malvertising and drive-by downloading.

Present-day cybercrimes and safeguards (courseware): hacking (black hat hackers break into networks to steal data or destroy resources; white hat hackers do so to find weaknesses and patch them); malware (for example a program infused into a retailer's server that harvests card numbers); identity theft (using another person's personal and financial information to buy, open accounts or borrow, without that person's permission); RAM scrapers (malware that captures data from random access memory, for example in point-of-sale machines); sniffing (viewing network traffic; password sniffing captures usernames and passwords); spoofing (a message sent from an unauthorised source claiming to be a trusted one); phishing (electronic communication posing as a trustworthy entity to get sensitive details; spear phishing targets a specific person or organisation; whaling aims at top management such as the CEO, CFO or CTO); smishing (phishing by SMS); vishing (voice phishing over VoIP, for example a call claiming an account is compromised); pharming (directing an internet user to a fake website to capture credentials and card data); zero-day vulnerability (a software vulnerability exploited before it is detected and patched); juice jacking (charging ports or infected cables used to steal data or load malware); remote access apps such as Anydesk used to take control of a victim's mobile. Safeguards: physical security (auto-lock with biometrics, PIN, password or pattern lock, SIM PIN, record IMEI and report loss); net security (check https and the padlock, check domain names and spelling, update operating systems, use reputable security software, avoid bogus schemes, use long strong passwords of upper and lower case, numbers and special characters, never share personal information publicly, report unauthorised transactions immediately to the bank and cyber cell); and two-factor authentication and strict password policies for organisations.

Payment fraud reporting (RBI Master Directions of 15 July 2024 and courseware): banks report payment-system related disputed, suspected or attempted fraudulent transactions to the Central Payments Fraud Information Registry (CPFIR) maintained by RBI; if such a transaction is subsequently concluded as a fraud committed on the bank, it must invariably be reported through the Fraud Monitoring Return (FMR) so that it is reflected in the Central Fraud Registry (CFR). The courseware adds that all RBI authorised payment system operators, providers and participants report all payment frauds including attempted incidents irrespective of value, that reporting moved from the Electronic Data Submission Portal to DAKSH, that the issuer bank, prepaid payment instrument issuer or credit card NBFC whose instrument was used submits the report, that entities validate the fraud information reported by customers, and that reporting is within 7 calendar days of the customer reporting or entity detection (courseware; the circular was not retrieved).

Governance structure for fraud risk management (RBI Master Directions of 15 July 2024): a Board approved policy on fraud risk management delineates the roles of the Board, Board committees and senior management; it covers prevention, early detection, investigation, staff accountability, monitoring, recovery and reporting; it includes measures for natural justice: a detailed show cause notice (SCN) to the persons, entities and their promoters and whole-time and executive directors against whom fraud is being examined, giving complete details of the transactions or events basis which a fraud declaration is contemplated; a reasonable time of not less than 21 days to respond; a well laid out system for issuing SCNs and examining responses before declaring fraud; and a reasoned Order served on the persons or entities conveying the decision to classify the account as fraud or otherwise, containing the relevant facts, the submissions against the SCN and the reasons. The policy is reviewed by the Board at least once in three years or more frequently. Banks constitute a Special Committee of the Board for Monitoring and Follow-up of cases of Frauds (SCBMF) with a minimum of three Board members, consisting of a whole-time director and a minimum of two independent or non-executive directors, headed by one of the independent or non-executive directors; the SCBMF oversees the effectiveness of fraud risk management, reviews and monitors cases of fraud including root cause analysis and suggests mitigating measures for internal controls, risk management and minimising fraud; the coverage and periodicity of reviews are decided by the Board. Senior management implements the policy and places a periodic review of fraud incidents before the Board or ACB. Banks have a transparent mechanism for whistle blower complaints on possible fraud and suspicious activities. A senior official in the rank of at least a General Manager or equivalent monitors and reports frauds within the fraud risk management structure (part of the overall risk management function).
facts.locator: RBI_FRM_2024 paragraphs 2.1 and 2.2; S01 printed pp. 671, 682-683

facts.statement: Early Warning Signals (EWS) and Red Flagging of Accounts (RFA) (RBI Master Directions of 15 July 2024): banks have an EWS and RFA framework under the Board approved fraud risk management policy; a Red Flagged Account is one where suspicion of fraudulent activity is thrown up by one or more EWS indicators, alerting deeper investigation from the potential fraud angle and initiating preventive measures. The Risk Management Committee of the Board (RMCB) oversees the framework, approves the EWS indicators and prescribes a turnaround time, preferably not more than 30 days, for examining EWS alerts; reviews the status of red flagged accounts at periodic intervals; and ensures the framework is validated. Senior management implements the framework. The framework provides for an EWS integrated with the core banking solution, timely remedial action, periodic review of sanction and monitoring processes, and effective use of CRILC and the Central Fraud Registry (not applicable to RRBs). For credit facilities the EWS is comprehensive with quantitative and qualitative indicators (transactional data, financial performance, market intelligence, borrower conduct) and banks set up a dedicated Data Analytics and Market Intelligence (MI) Unit; an EWS alert requires examination of whether the account needs to be red flagged. An account meeting the CRILC reporting threshold (aggregate fund-based and non-fund-based exposure of Rs 3 crore and above) once red flagged is reported to RBI within seven days. For other banking and non-credit transactions, banks strengthen EWS (including real-time monitoring and attention to non-KYC compliant and money mule accounts, and digital platform transactions); the EWS was to be upgraded within six months of the Directions. The courseware also lists many illustrative EWS indicators for loan accounts (for example default in statutory dues, bouncing of high value cheques, frequent change in project scope, heavy cash withdrawals, non-routing of sales proceeds, high value RTGS to unrelated parties, resignation of key personnel).
facts.locator: RBI_FRM_2024 paragraphs 3.1 to 3.5; S01 printed pp. 684-687

facts.statement: Red-flagged and fraud accounts, accountability and penal measures (RBI Master Directions of 15 July 2024): for a credit facility classified as a red-flagged account the bank uses an external audit or an internal audit, per its Board approved policy, to investigate further; banks frame a policy on engaging external auditors (due diligence, competency, track record; contracts with timelines) and loan agreements contain clauses for such audit; if the audit report is inconclusive or delayed by borrower non-cooperation the bank concludes on the available material and its own investigation. The decision to classify an account (standard or NPA) as red-flagged is taken at the individual bank level and reported on RBI's CRILC platform immediately, not later than seven days from classification. Natural justice is observed before declaring fraud. Once red flagged, classification as fraud or removal of the red flag is ordinarily completed within 180 days of first reporting on CRILC; cases beyond 180 days are reported to the SCBMF with adequate reasoning and are subject to supervisory review. If an account is identified as a fraud by any bank, the borrowal accounts of other group companies with common promoters or whole-time directors are examined by banks concerned from the fraud angle. If Law Enforcement Agencies have suo motu started an investigation involving a borrower account, banks immediately red-flag it and follow the usual process within the same period. Third-party service providers and professionals: agreements may hold them accountable where wilful negligence or malpractice caused the fraud; banks, after complying with natural justice, report such third parties to the Indian Banks Association, which circulates caution lists. Staff accountability: banks complete examination of staff accountability in all fraud cases in a time-bound manner; PSBs and AIFIs follow Central Vigilance Commission guidelines and refer all fraud cases involving Rs 3 crore and above, for examining the role of all levels of officials and whole-time directors (including ex-officials), to the CVC's Advisory Board for Banking and Financial Frauds (ABBFF); where very senior executives (MD and CEO, Executive Director or equivalent) are involved, the ACB initiates examination of accountability and places it before the Board (in PSBs and AIFIs also referred to the ABBFF). Penal measures: persons and entities classified and reported as fraud, and entities and persons associated with them, are debarred from raising funds or seeking additional credit facilities from financial entities regulated by RBI for five years from the date of full repayment of the defrauded amount or the agreed settlement amount; lending after the cooling period is at the lending bank's sole discretion. Resolution: if a fraud-classified entity undergoes resolution under the IBC or RBI's resolution framework with change in management and control, the bank examines whether the fraud classification continues; the penal measures do not apply to the entity after implementation of the resolution plan but continue to apply to the erstwhile promoters, directors and persons responsible, and criminal action continues against them.
facts.locator: RBI_FRM_2024 paragraphs 4.1 to 4.5; S01 printed pp. 686, 683

facts.statement: Reporting frauds to Law Enforcement Agencies (LEAs) (RBI Master Directions of 15 July 2024, Chapter V): banks immediately report incidents of fraud to LEAs, subject to applicable laws: private sector and foreign banks: below Rs 1 crore to State or Union Territory Police; Rs 1 crore and above, in addition to State or UT Police, to the Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO), Ministry of Corporate Affairs, with details reported in the Fraud Monitoring Return (FMR) format. Public sector banks and Regional Rural Banks: below Rs 6 crore to State or UT Police; Rs 6 crore and above to the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI). (The PSB threshold for CBI was raised from Rs 3 crore to Rs 6 crore as inflation indexed value.) In consortium lending each member may file separate complaints if separate offences were committed in respect of each, and in other cases only one member may file and the others support. Banks set up nodal points or designated officers for reporting to LEAs and coordination. The courseware also reproduces an older amount-wise table for lodging complaints (for example Rs 10,000 and above to State Police) which the 2024 Directions replaced.
facts.locator: RBI_FRM_2024 paragraphs 5.1 and 5.2; S01 printed pp. 688-689

facts.statement: Reporting frauds to RBI (RBI Master Directions of 15 July 2024, Chapter VI): to keep reporting uniform, banks choose the most appropriate FMR category from eleven: misappropriation of funds and criminal breach of trust; fraudulent encashment through forged instruments; manipulation of books of accounts or through fictitious accounts and conversion of property; cheating by concealment of facts with the intention to deceive any person and cheating by impersonation; forgery with the intention to commit fraud by making any false documents or electronic records; wilful falsification, destruction, alteration or mutilation of any book, electronic record, paper, writing, valuable security or account with intent to defraud; fraudulent credit facilities extended for illegal gratification; cash shortages on account of frauds; fraudulent transactions involving foreign exchange; fraudulent electronic banking or digital payment related transactions committed on banks; and other fraudulent activity not covered above. The Central Fraud Registry (CFR) is a web-based searchable database maintained by RBI, fed directly by banks' FMRs, and banks use it for credit risk and fraud risk management. Banks furnish the FMR in individual fraud cases, irrespective of the amount, immediately and not later than 14 days from the date of classification of an incident or account as fraud (updates through the FMR Update Application). Frauds at overseas branches are also reported to the overseas LEAs under host country law. Frauds in group entities (domestic and overseas subsidiaries, affiliates and joint ventures, financial or not) not regulated by a financial sector regulator are reported to RBI separately (by e-mail), and the group entities comply with natural justice before declaring fraud. Banks examine and fix staff accountability for delays in identification and reporting. Persons or entities not involved or associated with the fraud are not reported in the FMR. FMR can be withdrawn or names removed only in exceptional circumstances with due justification and approval of an official at least in the rank of a whole-time director. These reporting requirements do not apply to RRBs, which report to NABARD.
facts.locator: RBI_FRM_2024 paragraphs 6.1 to 6.3; S01 printed pp. 680-681

facts.statement: Closure, cheque frauds, legal audit, auditors and dates (RBI Master Directions of 15 July 2024): closure of fraud cases through the Closure Module requires that the cases pending with LEAs or courts are disposed of and the examination of staff accountability is completed; for limited statistical and reporting purposes banks may close reported fraud cases involving amounts up to Rs 1 crore (earlier Rs 25 lakh) where staff accountability examination and disciplinary action are done and either the investigation is going on or the charge-sheet has not been filed for more than three years from the date of registration of the FIR, or the charge-sheet is filed and the trial has not started or is pending for more than three years from registration of the FIR; details of closed cases are kept for auditors. Cheque related frauds: for forged instruments including fake or forged instruments sent in clearing in truncated form, reporting continues to be done by the paying banker and not the presenting banker, who hands over the instrument to the drawee bank on demand; where the instrument is genuine but payment has been made to a person who is not the true owner, or the amount was credited before realisation and the instrument was later found fake or forged and returned, the presenting bank that is defrauded files the fraud report with RBI and informs the LEAs. Legal audit: title deeds and other title documents for all credit facilities of Rs 5 crore and above are subject to periodic legal audit and re-verification until the loan is fully repaid (Rs 1 crore for Small Finance Banks, Local Area Banks and Regional Rural Banks), with scope and periodicity per the Board approved policy. Sale of fraud accounts: banks complete the investigation from the fraud angle before transferring a loan to other lenders or ARCs, and if they conclude a fraud has occurred they report it to RBI before the sale. Role of auditors: auditors who see possible fraudulent transactions immediately inform senior management and, if needed, the ACB; internal audit covers the controls and processes for prevention, detection, classification, monitoring, reporting, closure and withdrawal of fraud cases. Dates for FMR: the date of occurrence is when the actual misappropriation started or the event occurred as evidenced in audit or other findings; the date of detection is the actual date the fraud came to light in the branch, audit or department and not the date of approval by the competent authority; the date of classification is when due approval has been obtained from the competent authority for such classification and the reasoned order is passed. Theft, burglary, dacoity and robbery (including attempted cases) are reported to the Fraud Monitoring Group, Department of Supervision, RBI Central Office immediately and not later than seven days from occurrence, and a quarterly Return (RBR) covering all such cases in the quarter is submitted within 15 days of the end of the quarter.

Vigilance in banks (courseware): vigilance means being watchful and cautious to detect danger; in banks it ensures that public money held in fiduciary capacity is not misused and that transactions follow laid-down guidelines. There are three types: preventive vigilance (procedures and systems that restrain wrongdoing and misconduct, aimed at reducing the occurrence of a lapse), detective vigilance (scanning complaints, inspection and audit reports; detecting corrupt practices, malpractices, negligence and misconduct; close watch on officers at sensitive positions of doubtful integrity; scrutiny of decisions on discretionary powers) and punitive vigilance (investigation, collection of evidence, speedy departmental inquiries and swift, deterrent action against the real culprit). Preventive and detective vigilance deter a lapse; punitive vigilance is its complement, and a high penalty is ineffective if the quality of detection is poor. Preventive vigilance is organised by RBI's Central Vigilance Cell (CV Cell), which exercises jurisdiction over all employees and coordinates with the Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) and the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI). Objectives and measures of preventive vigilance include watchfulness and diligence by all employees; adherence to integrity and policies; planning and enforcement of regular inspections and audit; identification and location of sensitive areas; scrutiny of control returns; regular surprise visits to points susceptible to corrupt practices; regular transfer of officers and job rotation for award staff; close scrutiny of staff accounts; and surveillance of officers of doubtful integrity and those in the agreed list. Participative vigilance (courseware): vigilance should move from punitive and preventive to predictive, proactive and participative; every financial organisation has a Vigilance department headed by a Chief Vigilance Officer (CVO) reporting to the CMD or top executive; the CVC, set up in 1964 on the Santhanam Committee recommendation and given statutory status in 1998 after the Vineet Narain case, has restricted its jurisdiction to officers of Scale V and above in public sector banks.

Vigilance angle (RBI circular of 26 May 2011 and courseware): the vigilance angle is obvious in these acts: (i) demanding or accepting gratification other than legal remuneration in respect of an official act or for using influence with any other official; (ii) obtaining a valuable thing without consideration or with inadequate consideration from a person with whom the employee has or is likely to have official dealings or where influence can be exerted; (iii) obtaining for himself or herself or for any other person a valuable thing or pecuniary advantage by corrupt or illegal means or by abusing position as an employee; (iv) possession of assets disproportionate to known sources of income; and (v) cases of misappropriation, forgery or cheating or other similar criminal offences. For other irregularities such as gross or wilful negligence, recklessness in decision making, blatant violations of systems and procedures, exercise of discretion in excess where no ostensible organisational interest is evident, and failure to keep the controlling authority informed in time, the disciplinary authority with the help of the CIV (the CVO in public sector banks) studies the case and weighs the circumstances to decide whether there is reasonable ground to doubt the integrity of the officer. Once a case is registered as a vigilance case it is treated as such until its conclusion, irrespective of the outcome of the investigation; the CVO is authorised to decide the existence of a vigilance angle. The courseware adds a test of bona fides: whether a person of common prudence working within the prescribed rules and in the prevailing circumstances would have taken the decision in the commercial or operational interest of the organisation.

Origin of vigilance cases, CVO roles and disciplinary proceedings (courseware, CVC Vigilance Manual): information about corruption, malpractice or misconduct may reach the CVO from external and internal sources, in any form (oral, written, signed, anonymous or pseudonymous); verbal information is reduced to writing. Disposal of complaints is marked in the Vigilance Complaint Register as: filed without inquiry or investigation; filed after verification; passed on to the Complaints Cell as having no vigilance angle; passed on to the CBI; or taken up for detailed departmental investigation. The CVO's role is primarily preventive (periodically examining systems and procedures with functional departments to find loopholes) with a punitive role when malafides or charges of corruption are attributed during investigation (investigation to collect evidence, issue of charge sheet, holding of inquiry, consideration of the inquiry report, passing of penalty order), and a detective and surveillance role as the extended arm of the CVC. A departmental investigation (preliminary enquiry) is a fact-finding exercise and the current Government instruction is that it should be completed within 3 months; the employee is given an opportunity to tender his version during the investigation. As a general rule, no disciplinary proceeding ordinarily lies against an official for a lapse not detected within two regular audits or inspections of the same account or 4 years from the date of the event, whichever is later; this time limit does not apply to frauds, other criminal offences or cases where malafides are inferable. The Disciplinary Authority (DA) initiates action or recommends it, with independent and unbiased mind, on the CVO's advice; the standard of proof in a departmental enquiry is preponderance of probability and not proof beyond reasonable doubt; the Indian Evidence Act does not apply. The inquiry is quasi-judicial and follows natural justice: no one is condemned unheard, the accused is told the nature of accusations and is given an opportunity to rebut the prosecution evidence and prove innocence. The DA may impose a major or minor penalty or exonerate; the final order is a well-reasoned speaking order and the quantum of punishment is commensurate with the gravity of misconduct and consistent with the Service Rules. Major penalties for officers: reduction to a lower stage in the time scale of pay for a specific period; reduction to a lower grade or post; compulsory retirement; removal from service which is not a disqualification for future employment; and dismissal, which ordinarily is a disqualification for future employment. For award staff found guilty of gross misconduct, penalties include dismissal without notice, removal, compulsory retirement or discharge (each with or without superannuation benefits), reduction to a lower stage in the pay scale up to two stages for up to two years, withholding of increments, withdrawal of special pay or a warning or censure; a stiff or severe major penalty means removal, dismissal or compulsory retirement.

Twelve sutras for better fraud risk management (S S Mundra, courseware): (1) a robust fraud risk identification, event reporting, control, allocation and mitigation framework, with the four eyes principle in sensitive areas without compromise; (2) follow the 5 Cs of credit (Capacity, Capital, Collateral, Conditions and Character); (3) bring a culture of eternal vigilance, strong internal control and compliance, remembering that fraud is a criminal offence; (4) the solution for technological challenges is not always more technology; (5) institute checks and balances to calibrate people risk, with new recruits trained and given documented systems and rule books; (6) empower fraud risk managers adequately; (7) use extensively the 3 Cs: CFR (Central Fraud Registry), CRILC and credit bureaus; (8) rely on market intelligence; (9) develop business analytics tools; (10) cut losses and exit when the situation so demands; (11) do not throw good money after bad; and (12) comply with RBI regulations in letter and spirit.

RBI guidelines on internal vigilance for private sector and foreign banks (RBI circular of 26 May 2011): the guidelines align the vigilance function in private sector and foreign banks with that of public sector banks, to be put in place with Board approval within three months. The designated officer (similar to the CVO in public sector banks) is the Special Assistant or Advisor to the CEO and a liaison officer between the bank and the Police, SFIO and other law enforcement authorities. An officer of suitable seniority is designated Chief of Internal Vigilance (CIV) to head the Internal Vigilance Division; the CIV's functions broadly are (i) preventive vigilance, (ii) punitive vigilance and (iii) surveillance and detection: collecting intelligence on corrupt practices committed or likely to be committed by employees, investigating or causing investigation of verifiable allegations, processing investigation reports for the disciplinary authority, referring matters to the CEO for advice and taking steps to prevent improper practices. Preventive vigilance measures by the CIV: study procedures that give scope for corruption and the causes and points of delay; review regulatory functions; devise methods of control over the exercise of discretion; identify the areas prone to corruption and ensure officers of proven integrity are posted there. Appointment of the CIV is based on experience, track record, proven integrity and ability to inspire confidence. Tenure: the normal tenure is three years extendable up to a further two years; if the CIV shifts from one bank to another without completing the approved tenure in the previous bank, the principle of overall tenure of six years applies. Vigilance functionaries should not be party to processing and decision-making or other administrative transactions likely to have clear vigilance sensitivity; part-time functionaries confine other duties to items free from vigilance angle or that serve as input to vigilance activities such as inspection and audit. The CIV invariably reviews all pending matters (investigation reports, disciplinary cases, vigilance complaints) in the first week of every month; the Chief Executive holds periodic meetings to review vigilance work; and the CIV reports on vigilance activities to the Board or Local Governing Council periodically. Banks identify sensitive positions and frame a Board approved policy on staff rotation and mandatory leave (including a minimum period of mandatory leave for each category including the CEO). Any information about corruption, malpractice or misconduct of employees, from whatever source, is a complaint; sources include complaints from employees or the public, departmental inspection reports and stock verification surveys, scrutiny of annual property statements and of transactions reported under the Conduct Rules, irregularities detected in routine audit, audit reports, press reports, verbal source information from an identifiable source reduced to writing, and intelligence from agencies like the CBI; anonymous or pseudonymous complaints may be dealt with on merit. The bank decides whether to inquire departmentally or have a police investigation; no review is ordinarily made by the administrative authority of a case registered by the Police (the Police are associated if special reasons arise); action is considered against the complainant if a complaint is malicious, vexatious or unfounded; and the CIV maintains close liaison with the police and SFIO through periodic meetings.

payload.title: What fraud means and how the law defines it
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Fraud** is **intentional deception to secure unfair or unlawful gain**, directly or indirectly. It can be a **civil wrong** or a **criminal offence**, depending on context and severity.

| Source | Core idea (courseware) |
| --- | --- |
| **Contract Act, 1872, s.17** | Acts done with **intent to deceive** a party or **induce** a contract: **false suggestion of fact**, **active concealment**, **promise made with no intention to perform**, **any other act fitted to deceive**, **any act or omission the law declares fraudulent**. **Mere silence is not fraud** unless there is a **duty to speak** or the silence **equals speech** |
| **Companies Act, 2013, s.447 (explanation)** | **Any act, omission, concealment of fact or abuse of position**, by any person or with connivance, **with intent to deceive, gain undue advantage or injure** the company, shareholders, creditors or any other person, **whether or not there is wrongful gain or loss** |
| **IPC s.25, now BNS s.2(9)** | Doing a thing **"fraudulently"**: with **intent to defraud** and not otherwise |

**Wrongful gain** is gain by **unlawful means** of property one is **not legally entitled** to; **wrongful loss** is loss by unlawful means of property one **is** legally entitled to. **Intent to defraud** is **paramount**: defraud means **deceit and injury**.

The **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023** replaced the **IPC from 1 July 2024**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Under the Companies Act explanation, fraud exists even when no wrongful gain or loss results, as long as there is intent to deceive.

self_check.prompt_text: Is mere silence fraud under the Contract Act explanation?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Not by itself; only if there is a duty to speak or the silence is equivalent to speech.

payload.title: Forgery and the false document
payload.core_explanation_md:
Held at needs_review (courseware's IPC-era account).

**Forgery** is **creating a false written document** or **altering a genuine one** with **intent to defraud**.

- The offence is **complete once the document is made** with intent to commit fraud.
- The document **need not be in the name of a real person**: a **fictitious or deceased** person is enough.
- If **several persons combine** to forge, **each who takes a distinct part is guilty**.
- **Counterfeiting** a document to support a **legal claim** is forgery.
- **Antedating** is forgery if the **date is material**.
- A document made to **conceal a previous fraudulent or dishonest act** is forgery, but falsification only to conceal a **previous negligent act** is **not**.
- A man's **signature of his own name** can amount to forgery.
- Forgery can be **abetted**.
- **Affixing an electronic signature** carries the meaning in the **Information Technology Act, 2000**.

**Equivalents today:** IPC **463 (forgery)** is now **BNS 336(1)**; IPC **464 (making a false document)** is **BNS 335**.

payload.title: The main cyber threats
payload.core_explanation_md:
A **cyber-attack** is an **intentional, malicious effort** to breach another's systems for **information theft, financial gain, espionage or sabotage**.

| Threat | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **DDoS** (distributed denial of service) | **Overwhelms** the target so it **stops functioning**; often a **diversion** for subtler attacks |
| **Social engineering** | **Manipulates users psychologically**: **phishing**, **spear phishing**, **homograph attacks** |
| **Man-in-the-middle** | Attacker sits **between user and server**: **session hijacking**, **replay**, **IP spoofing**, **eavesdropping** |
| **Malware and spyware** | **Trojan**; **ransomware** (blocks data, demands payment); **malvertising** (malicious code in ads) |
| **Password attacks** | **Sniffing**, **social engineering**, **guessing**, **password database access** |
| **APT** (advanced persistent threat) | **Long-term, undetected access** to exfiltrate data, typically against **states or big corporations** |

**Ransomware** and **identity theft** are the other two major threats. **Crypto ransomware** **encrypts** files; computers are commonly infected via **phishing e-mail attachments or links**, **malvertising** and **drive-by downloading**.

payload.title: Present-day cybercrimes and safeguards
payload.core_explanation_md:
| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Hacking** | **Black hat** breaks in to **steal or destroy**; **white hat** does it to **find and patch weaknesses** |
| **Phishing** | Communication **posing as a trusted entity** to obtain sensitive data; **spear phishing** targets **one person or organisation**; **whaling** targets **top management** |
| **Smishing / Vishing** | Phishing by **SMS** / by **voice (VoIP) call** |
| **Pharming** | Directing a user to a **fake website** to capture credentials |
| **Sniffing / Spoofing** | **Viewing network traffic** (password sniffing) / a message sent **from an unauthorised source posing as a trusted one** |
| **RAM scraper** | Malware that **captures data from memory**, e.g. in **POS machines** |
| **Zero-day vulnerability** | A flaw **exploited before it is detected and patched** |
| **Juice jacking** | **Charging ports or cables** used to **steal data or load malware** |
| **Identity theft** | Using another's **personal and financial information** without permission |

**Safeguards:** **lock devices** (biometric, PIN, pattern, SIM PIN), note the **IMEI**; check **https and the padlock**, **domain spelling**; **update software**; use **reputable security software**; **long strong passwords**; **never share data publicly**; report unauthorised transactions at once to the **bank and cyber cell**; organisations use **two-factor authentication** and strict password policies.

If a transaction is **later concluded to be a fraud on the bank**, it is **invariably reported through the FMR** (Fraud Monitoring Return) so that it appears in the **Central Fraud Registry (CFR)**.

**Courseware (needs_review):** payment system operators, providers and participants report **all payment frauds including attempted ones, irrespective of value**; reporting has moved from the **Electronic Data Submission Portal** to **DAKSH**; the **issuer bank, PPI issuer or credit card NBFC** whose instrument was used reports; entities **validate customer-reported information**; reports within **7 calendar days** of the customer's report or the entity's detection.

payload.title: Early warning signals and red flagging of accounts
payload.core_explanation_md:
A **red flagged account (RFA)** is one where **one or more early warning signal (EWS) indicators** raise **suspicion of fraud**, triggering **deeper investigation from the fraud angle** and **preventive measures**.

| Element | Rule (RBI Master Directions, 15 July 2024) |
| --- | --- |
| **Who oversees** | **Risk Management Committee of the Board (RMCB)**: approves **EWS indicators**, reviews red flagged accounts, ensures **validation** |
| **Turnaround time** | **Preferably not more than 30 days** to examine an EWS alert |
| **Systems** | EWS **integrated with core banking**; **timely remedial action**; use of **CRILC and the Central Fraud Registry** |
| **Credit accounts** | **Quantitative and qualitative indicators** (transaction data, financial performance, market intelligence, conduct); a **Data Analytics and Market Intelligence (MI) Unit** |
| **CRILC reporting** | Account with **aggregate exposure (fund and non-fund based) of Rs 3 crore or more**: report to RBI **within 7 days** of red flagging |
| **Non-credit transactions** | Strengthen EWS (real-time monitoring; **non-KYC compliant and money mule accounts**; **digital platforms**) |

**Illustrative EWS (courseware):** default in **statutory dues**, **bouncing of high value cheques**, **frequent change in project scope**, **heavy cash withdrawals**, **sales proceeds not routed**, **high value RTGS to unrelated parties**, **resignation of key personnel**.

payload.title: Red-flagged accounts, accountability and penal measures
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Red-flagged credit account:** investigate by **external audit** or **internal audit** per Board policy (frame a **policy for external auditors**; put **audit clauses in loan agreements**). If the audit is **inconclusive or delayed by the borrower**, the bank decides **on the material available and its own investigation**.

**Reporting and timing:**

- the **individual bank** decides on red flagging (standard or NPA) and reports on **CRILC within 7 days**;
- classification as fraud or **removal of the flag** is ordinarily done **within 180 days** of first CRILC reporting; longer cases go to the **SCBMF** and are subject to **supervisory review**;
- **natural justice** applies before declaring fraud.

**Wider checks:** if one bank classifies a fraud, **group companies with common promoters or whole-time directors** are examined; if **LEAs start investigating on their own**, the bank **red-flags immediately** and follows the same process.

**Third parties:** contracts can hold **service providers and professionals** accountable for wilful negligence or malpractice; after natural justice, they are reported to the **Indian Banks Association** for **caution lists**.

**Staff accountability:** examined in **all** fraud cases, in a **time-bound** manner. **PSBs and AIFIs** follow **CVC guidelines** and refer fraud cases of **Rs 3 crore or more** to the CVC's **Advisory Board for Banking and Financial Frauds (ABBFF)**; for **MD and CEO or Executive Director-level** involvement the **ACB** starts the examination and the Board considers it.

**Penal measures:** persons and entities classified as fraud, and **associated** entities and persons, are **debarred for five years** from raising funds or **seeking additional credit** from RBI-regulated entities, counted from the **date of full repayment or agreed settlement**; lending afterwards is at the bank's **sole discretion**.

**After resolution:** if an entity under **IBC or RBI's resolution framework** changes management and control, the bank **examines whether the fraud classification continues**; **penal measures do not apply to the resolved entity** but **continue against erstwhile promoters and directors**, with **criminal action** continuing.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The five-year cooling period runs from full repayment, so settlement amounts matter.

The PSB threshold for the CBI was raised from **Rs 3 crore** to **Rs 6 crore** as an **inflation indexed** value.

**Consortium lending:** each member may file **separately** if **separate offences** were committed against each; otherwise **one member files** and the others **support**.

Banks appoint **nodal officers** for reporting and coordination with LEAs. The courseware's older table (for example Rs 10,000 and above to State Police) is **superseded**.

payload.title: Vigilance in banks: types and aims
payload.core_explanation_md:
Held at needs_review (courseware).

**Vigilance** ensures that **public money held in fiduciary capacity** is **not misused** and that transactions follow **laid-down guidelines**.

| Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Preventive** | **Procedures and systems that restrain wrongdoing**, reducing lapses |
| **Detective** | **Scanning complaints, inspection and audit reports**; **watch on officers at sensitive positions** and **their discretionary decisions** |
| **Punitive** | **Investigation, evidence, speedy departmental inquiry**, **swift deterrent action** |

Preventive and detective vigilance **deter** lapses; punitive vigilance **complements** them. A high penalty is **ineffective** if **detection is poor**.

**Preventive measures:** **watchfulness by all staff**, **adherence to integrity and policies**, **planned inspections and audit**, **identify sensitive areas**, **scrutinise control returns**, **surprise visits**, **regular transfers and job rotation**, **close scrutiny of staff accounts**, **surveillance of officers of doubtful integrity (the agreed list)**.

**Institutions:** RBI's **Central Vigilance Cell** coordinates with the **CVC** and **CBI**; each bank has a **Vigilance department** under a **Chief Vigilance Officer (CVO)**. The **CVC** was set up in **1964** (Santhanam Committee), became **statutory in 1998**, and **restricts its jurisdiction to Scale V and above** in public sector banks.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware says vigilance should become predictive, proactive and participative, not only punitive.

payload.title: Vigilance cases, investigation and disciplinary proceedings
payload.core_explanation_md:
Held at needs_review (courseware, CVC Vigilance Manual).

**Origin:** information from **any source and in any form** (oral, written, signed, anonymous, pseudonymous); **verbal information is written down**.

**Disposal of complaints** in the Vigilance Complaint Register: **filed without inquiry**; **filed after verification**; **passed to the Complaints Cell (no vigilance angle)**; **passed to the CBI**; **taken up for detailed departmental investigation**.

**CVO's roles:** **preventive** (examining systems with departments to find loopholes), **punitive** (investigation, charge sheet, inquiry, consideration of the report, penalty order) and **detective and surveillance** as the **extended arm of the CVC**.

**Preliminary enquiry:** **fact finding**, to be completed **within 3 months**; the employee may tender his version.

**Time limit:** no disciplinary proceeding **ordinarily** for a lapse not detected within **two regular audits or inspections** of the account, or **4 years from the event**, **whichever is later**; **not** for **frauds**, **other criminal offences** or **inferable malafides**.

**Disciplinary Authority (DA):** decides **independently**, on the **CVO's advice**; the standard of proof is **preponderance of probability** (not beyond reasonable doubt); the **Evidence Act does not apply**.

**Inquiry:** **quasi-judicial**; **natural justice**: **no one condemned unheard**, **told the accusations**, **opportunity to rebut and prove innocence**. The final order is a **well-reasoned speaking order**; punishment is **proportionate** and **consistent**.

**Major penalties (officers):** **reduction to a lower stage in the pay scale**, **reduction to a lower grade or post**, **compulsory retirement**, **removal** (not a disqualification for future employment) and **dismissal** (ordinarily a disqualification).
payload.expanded_explanation_md: For award staff the penalties also include discharge, reduction up to two stages for up to two years, withholding increments, withdrawal of special pay, warning or censure.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the standard of proof in a departmental enquiry?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Preponderance of probability, not proof beyond reasonable doubt.

payload.title: Internal vigilance in private sector and foreign banks (RBI, 26 May 2011)
payload.core_explanation_md:
The RBI aligned the vigilance function of **private sector and foreign banks** with that of PSBs, to be set up **with Board approval within three months**.

**Chief of Internal Vigilance (CIV):** an officer of **suitable seniority** heads the **Internal Vigilance Division** and acts as **Special Assistant or Advisor to the CEO** and **liaison with Police, SFIO and other agencies** (like a CVO in PSBs). The CIV's functions: **preventive**, **punitive**, **surveillance and detection**.

| Topic | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| **Appointment** | Based on **experience, track record, proven integrity, ability to inspire confidence** |
| **Tenure** | **Three years, extendable up to two more**; if moving between banks without completing the term, **six years overall** applies |
| **Sensitive matters** | Vigilance staff **not party to processing or decision-making** with **vigilance sensitivity**; part-timers keep other duties **free of vigilance angle** (or inputs such as inspection and audit) |
| **Review** | CIV reviews **all pending matters in the first week of every month**; Chief Executive holds **periodic review meetings**; CIV **reports to the Board or Local Governing Council** periodically |
| **Staff rotation and mandatory leave** | **Board approved policy** for **sensitive positions**, with **minimum rotation period** and **minimum mandatory leave for each category including the CEO** |

**Preventive vigilance (CIV):** study procedures that give scope for corruption and causes of delay; **review regulatory functions**; **control discretion**; **identify corruption-prone areas and post officers of proven integrity there**.

**Complaints:** **any information about corruption, malpractice or misconduct from any source**; sources include **employees or the public**, **inspection reports and stock surveys**, **annual property statements**, **Conduct Rules transactions**, **routine audit irregularities**, **press reports**, **verbal information from an identifiable source (written down)** and **agency intelligence**; **anonymous or pseudonymous complaints can be dealt with on merit**.

**Investigation:** decide **departmental inquiry or police investigation**; **no ordinary review of a police-registered case** by the administration (association of Police if needed); consider **action against malicious, vexatious or unfounded complainants**; **close liaison with Police and SFIO** through periodic meetings.
